story_text.value:
A stem splitter I built. Upload a song and get vocals (lead and backing), instrumental, drums, bass, guitar, piano, or even the drums split into kick, snare, toms, hi-hat and the rest. You pay per minute of audio with credits (while also being cheaper than other competitors), and there's a free daily allowance (with an account, I don't want it to be abused), and downloads/stems aren't locked behind a paid tier. You can listen to the example on the landing page if you don't want to sign up yet. There's also a pretty easy-to-use API, if you want to integrate it with your own tools. You also don't have to know anything at all about the underlying models either, because there's no complicated list to pick from.

And no, it's not just an HTDemucs wrapper, it runs the current top open models with some tuning on top. Any feedback is appreciated!

story_text.value:
I built the tool for local businesses, I know they have the problem: getting one built is easy, but nobody touches it afterwards. Content goes outdated - working hours wrong, photos on the website from 2019 and reviews customers leaving on different platforms are everywhere but not on the website.

My tool helps to build website in one click: you type a business name it reads the reviews and photos from Google, Yelp, Tripadvisor and builds a website from them in a few minutes, then it keeps reading and updating contnet constantly

- A worker re-reads Google and other platforms on a schedule, stores only what is new, and rewrites the copy - Owners change things by chatting ("make it dark green", "add a page about emergency repairs")

A while ago I've also built a bunch of free tools that are on the website and are open source: https://github.com/vaitko/locan-tools

I'd like to hear where the generated sites look wrong or generic.

Thank you for your feedback!

story_text.value:
Hi everyone. I'm an AI Masters student (UvA Amsterdam), and quite the geography nerd, having spent countless hours on GeoGuessr. I wanted to make my own simple geography game, but with some (even small) AI component to it.

The game consists of 6 geography-related questions (countries, capitals, flags, languages, borders, etc) every day, where the rarer your answer, the rarer your score (tiers are [common, uncommon, rare, ultra rare, legendary]). No account needed or anything.

Something I didn't expect to cause so many issues were definitions. What counts as a country? A territory? When does a country 'speak' a language? I would set a definition, and players would always (justifiably so!) break it -> "Well OK then if this is the definition, how come you don't accept [very obscure super borderline answer]". Eventually I converged on a happy-medium with enough inclusion (I think), without the definition being a whole paragraph long:

(i) Country: a sovereign state. Niue and the Cook Islands still cause problems: the UN lists them as "non-member states", but they exhibit quite a bit of sovereignty, so I count them as countries.

(ii) Territory: a place with an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code, given or reserved, that isn't a sovereign state (e.g., Heard Island and McDonald Islands, Sint Maarten, Sark,...)

(iii) Language spoken in {country}: working or official language, as said so by the government (or the entity's governing body)

Two components I think would be interesting for Show HN, and would like feedback on, are how I determine an answer's rarity and the day's difficulty.

Difficulty: I trained a linear regression model on past play data (30 days, currently) to predict a number between 0 and 1. For each of the first 5 questions (the 6th is different in nature), I gather 3 features for the regression model: ln(num. possible answers), ln(1 + num. 'common' answers), and whether answers contain a 'legandary' (0 or 1), then take the weighted average. Fixed cut-offs snap that into a 1-5 difficulty level (e.g., 4/5).

Rarity (e.g, "Name a country in the EU" -> Belgium):

(i) Fame. Using Google Books Ngram (how often the name appears in English), QRank (pageviews of the name's wikidata item, summed over every wikipedia language), and Wikipedia page views (median yearly views), I calculate a "Fame Score" for every country, territory, and capital (e.g., USA: 7.18, France: 6.85, Tuvalu: 5.76)

(ii) Weight. Sometimes rarities still don't feel quite right, so every question template (e.g., "Name a country in Europe") gets a weight based on how much information it gives the player. Luxembourg is valid for both "Name a country" and "Name a country in Europe", but knowing it's in Europe narrows your possibilities, making Luxembourg an "easier" answer for the latter.

(iii) Multiply Fame times the Weight to get a rarity score from 0-100, snapped to one of the rarity tiers.

It's a side project, and I'm continuously improving things based on feedback from players emailing me. Perhaps some of you could also provide some feedback?

1. How did the game 'feel' to you? 2. Were any of your answers rejected? 3. What is something you like about the game? 4. What is something you dislike about the game? 5. Any other miscellaneous observations/suggestions/bugs

Anything is appreciated. Thank you for your read, and have a good day/night!

title.value: Show HN: Daily Atlas, my geography quiz game where rarer answers score more

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

this is Collection of Beauty, a walkable, multi-floor 3D museum, based on a collection of art that I handpicked with 4000+ works.

History: I've spent some time earlier this year just browsing Wikipedia public domain art for literally hours on end, downloading everything that I liked or appreciated, just asking myself do I find this beautiful on some level?

The result is this... Well, not quite ^^

In the end I had a large folder with a bunch of images in it that begged the question: can I make this more useful somehow? Like, it's nice to have all these images sitting on my hard disk somehow but I want to share this with other people as a Collection of Beauty. But they were just images, nothing else.

A bit of wrangling with AI later and now this website exists. It has a 3D museum you can walk through, with multiple floors. The images are displayed at their real sizes relative to one another and the room layouts etc. And yes, the Mona Lisa is that small ^^

Luckily Wikimedia file names can be reverse searched and therefore I had access to the entire Wikimedia metadata against each of the images to sort them and create a metadata catalogue that allows for different ways of slicing through the images, like showing things like: "similar artists", "other artists the artist knew personally", or just "epoch/style" related ideas. I also sorted paintings by color on one of the sub pages, because I thought that would be nifty.

If you find something that is clearly in the wrong epoch or by the wrong artist or the wrong size, has a wrong title or whatever, please file an issue on GitHub (https://github.com/trebeljahr/collection-of-beauty).

Also I know of this other project that did something similar (though they mapped literally all art that ever existed), but I swear I had this idea on my own, sometimes different people come up with the same stuff. https://artmuseum.artfrompixels.com/ When a friend sent this to me, I took some inspiration though and made the frames and lighting and general 3D experience much more beautiful as well. I also had to facepalm myself and whisper: "why didn't I think of this myself," and then added some (public domain or freely licensed) music playing in the background as you look at the paintings.

The whole thing is deployed with Cloudflare workers because it's 90% static and Cloudflare has very very generous free tiers.

Also credit where credit is due, the set of flowers from Redoute is from https://www.c82.net/redoute/ one of my favorite websites of all time ^^

Under the hood the image rendering in the 3D walkthrough does something cool with LOD texture variants where rooms determine when to load each painting's resolution based on a bunch of heuristics, keeping the experience relatively lightweight and fast (hopefully). It should load the really big scans only if you jam up your nose right into a painting.

If some beautiful but more modern art is missing (MC Escher?!) then this is because of copyright issues. There are quite a few artists whose work I would love to include in here but where there is still copyright on the images and therefore I can't afaik.

Also, if you have more Public Domain art, that you personally really like, please share that with me too, would love to include more stuff in here (if I like it ofc ^^). Link to Wikipedia, name of the artist to check out, name of the painting, etc.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I wanted something like workerd + celld for untrusted Rust apps and couldn’t find anything that quite fit. That said, I got a lot of inspiration from workerd, celld, spin, and wasmcloud.

spared (spare-dee) runs Rust apps + SQLite in isolated WASM sandboxes. It lets you run many apps per server, and by packaging SQLite inside the sandbox, you get better isolation than running it on the host. This opens the door to running untrusted code on a single machine.

It's open source and runs on any VPS.

It's still early, and there's still a lot to build, but it feels like it's at a good place to share. Let me know what you think.

Repo: https://github.com/michaelmagan/spared

story_text.value:
I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend.

Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control.

We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine.

We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider.

Keep the SES integration

For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration:

  import boto3
  
  ses = boto3.client(
      "sesv2",
      region_name="us-east-1",
      endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com",
  )
For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/

Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix

In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery.

  Engine                Messages per second
  NitroMTA              3,313
  KumoMTA               1,048
  Postfix with OpenDKIM  806
Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it.

The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid.

KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately.

The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/

Give each IP a budget for each provider

An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off.

We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it.

With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung.

The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable.

Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records.

Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

story_text.value:
I tend to make a lot of scratch notes as a way to help me think. These usually don't last very long and what does survive usually ends up in a git repo, a wiki or (most often) just gets thrown away.

I was using Obsidian for this, but gosh, 4 or 5 Electron processes just for throwaway notes seemed like overkill. Neovim is a better fit but I like it just the way it is for coding and didn't want to install any image plug-ins for that.

mib is a bit like a basic Vim editor, with a few Obsidian features cherry-picked and a workflow optimized around scratch notes (with just 9 glorious pages - no files or folders to organize).

It's called "mib" because it is, and always will be under 1MiB (currently < 300KiB). Its a fully local, native app that is smaller than some JavaScript frameworks.

Disclosure: I still write a lot of code by hand but this project is 100% AI generated (Claude and Codex). I was a tough taskmaster though - we worked through a lot of approaches to arrive at something this small.
